This started out as a response to another post regarding hunting, but I thought I'd spread some knowledge on hunting.

Hunting is more than an excuse to own firearms, a reason become a proficient marksman, a way to obtain cheep meats, and a unique way to experience and participate in the natural world. It is a vital part of environmental conservation in areas with modern human habitation.

Recreational hunters are true eco warriors. No, really. They do more for the environment than 99% of environmental activists. What most people don't understand is that the purpose of hunting, at least in the majority of the US, is to mitigate damage to the environment that we have already caused.

Modern human habitation has pushed most other apex predators into near extinction. This has in turn thoroughly fucked the natural mechanisms that have balanced the populations of prey species for the millions of years before we started to get our shit together.

Responsible hunting replaces the predation pressure vacuum left by the apex predators we've driven from most of the environments we inhabit. Without predation pressure, the populations of prey spike until they reach a critical mass. Then they all run out of food and die off to dangerously low levels. This in turn fucks with plant life, because they're eating all of their food, meaning fewer seeds for the next year, right? This creates a feedback loop that can, has and will result in extinctions.

Hunting, when properly managed by a government that knows WTF it's doing, creates a stabilizing effect on wildlife populations and works to counteract the feedback loops I just mentioned.

If we didn't have men and women who enjoyed hunting recreationally, many governments would be forced to pay people to do it. I'm not kidding, there have been instances where governments have been forced to pay people to shoot deer from helicopters.

Ecology is a complicated topic, and its hard to describe how dangerous to the environment such feedback loops are. Read the wikipedia article on keystone species if you're interested in learning more. When you do, keep in mind that it's surprisingly difficult to know whether a species is a keystone species or not until it's too late.
